SUBJECT: Frances Kowalski, 89
INTERVIEWER: Linda (daughter)
SETTING: Frances's kitchen, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. Session 1.
PROFILE NOTES: Born 1937, Polish-American. Father worked at Bethlehem Steel. Worked the lunch counter at Woolworth's in the 1950s. Married Eddie Kowalski. Three children (Linda, Carol, Michael). Some memory loss in the past two years.

Q: Ma, can you tell me about the house on — what was it, Fourth Street?

A: Fourth Street. Yes. Well, we — it was my father's house. No, my grandmother's. It was my grandmother's house and we all — there was a porch. Is that thing on? [laughs] Linda, is it on? Okay. So there was the porch and the, um, the... my father would sit there. After. He'd come home all black. Black from the — from the plant. And my mother wouldn't let him in the kitchen until he washed at the... there was a sink, out back, by the coal. By the coal bin. Cold water. Even in winter, cold water.

Q: What about your mother? What did she do?

A: Oh, she kept house. Everybody's mother kept house then. She was a good woman. Very religious. We went to church every Sunday, St. Stanislaus, everybody did. She was a good mother. She worked hard. They all worked hard then, people don't know.

Q: Do you remember anything she used to cook?

A: Pierogi. Well. Everybody says pierogi. [pause] She had — her hands were always red. From the, uh, the lye soap. She'd make the dough and her knuckles would crack, right here, and she'd put lard on them. Lard! Can you imagine. Rub it in like hand cream. [pause] I don't know why I remember that.

Q: Tell me about meeting Dad.

A: Eddie. Eddie was — we met at the dance, at the, the Sokol hall. He had that car. A Ford. A green — no. No, it was his brother's car, he didn't have a car. [pause] Or was that Walt? Walt had the car. Walt had the green car. [pause] I went with Walt first, you know. Before your father. For a while. Don't put that in.

Q: Okay, Ma, we won't. What year did you and Dad get married?

A: Fifty... fifty-six. No. Fifty-eight. Your brother was born in fifty-nine, so — [pause] Fifty-eight. June. It rained.

Q: What do you remember about the wedding?

A: Well, my father, you know, he'd come home from the plant and he'd wash out back. My mother wouldn't let him in. There was a sink down in the cellar, by the coal, and he'd wash there with the cold water, even in the winter. Black. All black from the plant. [pause] Did I tell you that?

Q: You did, Ma. We were talking about the wedding.

A: Were we? Oh. Well, it rained. Everybody said rain was lucky. [pause] Is your sister coming today? [Linda: Ma, Carol's in Arizona.] Oh, that's right. That's right. She told me. She called. [pause] What were we saying?

Q: Tell me about working at Woolworth's.

A: Oh, I loved that. I loved it. The lunch counter. Grilled cheese was thirty-five cents. Or — no, a quarter. A quarter, I think. And the steel men would come in at the shift change, all at once, you had to have the coffee ready, forty cups lined up on the counter, because they'd only have — they had fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes and then back. And there was one, he always left a nickel under the saucer. Every day. Never said a word. Every single day, a nickel under the saucer. I never knew his name.

Q: Why did you stop working there?

A: Well, when you get married, you — [long pause] I don't remember. I don't. Isn't that terrible? [pause] I don't know why I stopped. I liked it there.

Q: That's okay, Ma. It doesn't matter.

A: My father. When he washed out back, by the coal — he'd sing. Did I tell you that? He sang in Polish. Every night, washing. I don't know the words. I never learned. My mother didn't want us talking Polish, she wanted us to be American. [pause] I wish I knew the words.
